Attributable risk: excess incidence among exposed attributable to exposure, assuming causality
HR: survival analysis with censoring; constant interpretation assumes proportional hazards

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Use proportions, not percentage numbers, in reciprocal calculations
OR approximates RR only with rare outcomes; common outcomes exaggerate relative association
Association alone cannot establish causality; confounding can distort every measure

measures-of-association.evidence: Statistical definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.name: Medical errors and patient safety
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.scope: Near miss, adverse event, error disclosure, root cause analysis, structured sign-outs and handoffs
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.core: Protect the patient first, disclose errors honestly, and redesign systems to reduce recurrence.

rows.label: Principle
items: Just culture: distinguish human error, risky shortcuts, and reckless conduct
Psychological safety enables reporting; accountability and system improvement can coexist
Effective communication: bedside verbal handoff with patient → real-time feedback, shared mental model

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Stabilize and mitigate harm**, notify supervising clinician, preserve relevant clinical information
★ Disclose facts, consequences, **apology**, treatment/prevention plans; update uncertainties
★ Report through institutional safety system; document clinical facts and disclosure in medical record

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid concealment, altered records, premature blame, or speculation about causation
Do not rely on education alone when workflow permits predictable repeated errors
Do not trust result delivery alone (fax, mail); **test-tracking log** verifies receipt, review, follow-up

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Reckless impairment/dangerous conduct → remove from unsafe duties; institutional escalation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Root cause analysis**: retrospective system investigation; identify multiple contributors
Failure mode and effects analysis: prospective hazard assessment before harm
Handoff: standardized I-PASS/SBAR, pending tasks, contingency plans, receiver synthesis/read-back

table.title: Event classification
rows: Unanticipated death/serious harm/life-saving rescue; prompts RCA
Upstream scheduling/staffing flaw; fix system, not individual

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.evidence: Not checked online; established patient-safety terminology and ethical disclosure principles.

menopause.name: Menopause
menopause.scope: Perimenopause, menopause transition, vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, HRT
menopause.core: Menopause is 12 months without menses from ovarian follicle depletion; manage bothersome symptoms according to uterine status and hormone-treatment risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Natural transition typically in late 40s–50s; smoking, oophorectomy, chemotherapy or pelvic radiation accelerate onset
Menopause before 40 suggests primary ovarian insufficiency and requires a separate evaluation

rows.label: Clues
items: Perimenopause: variable cycles, skipped periods, fertility remains; isolated irregularity → **reassurance**, no biopsy
Vasomotor episodes: abrupt heat, flushing, sweating, disturbed sleep; mood symptoms can coexist
Genitourinary syndrome: dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency and recurrent UTIs; pale thin friable mucosa
Urogenital estrogen loss: **negative cultures**, possible sterile pyuria; friable mucosa → spotting, postcoital bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ↓Follicles → ↓estradiol/inhibin and ↑FSH; hypothalamic thermoregulatory changes drive hot flashes
Urogenital estrogen deficiency thins epithelium, raises vaginal pH and changes flora

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms at **≥45 years → clinical diagnosis**; routine FSH unnecessary
Unexpected amenorrhea → pregnancy test; earlier menopause → FSH/estradiol and targeted thyroid/prolactin evaluation
Postmenopausal bleeding → endometrial evaluation; do not attribute to normal transition
Hormonal contraception alters bleeding/FSH interpretation; amenorrhea on contraception alone does not establish menopause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bothersome hot flashes, low risk, generally <60 or within 10 years → **systemic estrogen**
★ Intact uterus → **add progestogen**; hysterectomy → estrogen alone usually sufficient
Avoid systemic hormones with unexplained bleeding, estrogen-sensitive cancer, prior VTE/stroke/MI or active liver disease
Hormones unsuitable → **venlafaxine, paroxetine or gabapentin**; selected fezolinetant requires liver monitoring
★ Isolated GSM → lubricants/moisturizers then **low-dose vaginal estrogen**; routine progestogen generally unnecessary

rows.label: Complications
items: Bone loss, fracture, sexual dysfunction; oral systemic estrogen increases VTE/stroke risk
Combined systemic hormones can increase breast cancer risk; unopposed uterine estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight-bearing exercise, adequate calcium/vitamin D, smoking cessation; age/risk-based osteoporosis screening
Hormone treatment not for primary cardiovascular/dementia prevention; reassess symptoms and risks periodically
Continue contraception during transition until menopause criteria met; menopausal hormones do not prevent pregnancy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent heat intolerance, tachycardia, suppressed TSH
Pregnancy: positive hCG despite irregular cycles

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.scope: MEN1 (pituitary, parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic neuroendocrine), MEN2A (medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid), MEN2B (medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas), RET gene
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.core: Autosomal dominant syndromes with characteristic combinations of endocrine tumors, often multifocal and presenting young.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Affected relatives, young-onset endocrine tumor, multifocal disease, or multiple endocrine organs involved

rows.label: Clues
items: MEN1: hypercalcemia, recurrent ulcers or hypoglycemia, galactorrhea or visual field loss
MEN2B: marfanoid habitus and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis; early aggressive thyroid disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ MEN1: loss of menin tumor suppressor; MEN2: activating **RET** proto-oncogene variant

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Germline testing when phenotype suggests MEN; offer cascade testing to relatives
MEN1: calcium/PTH, prolactin and symptom-directed hormone assays; pancreatic and pituitary imaging
MEN2: calcitonin for medullary disease; plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines for pheochromocytoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pheochromocytoma → **alpha blockade then adrenal surgery before thyroid surgery**; beta blockade only after alpha
MEN1: multigland parathyroid surgery, cabergoline for prolactinoma, individualized pancreatic NET management

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypercalcemic nephrolithiasis, pituitary mass effects, metastatic NET or medullary thyroid cancer
Unrecognized pheochromocytoma → perioperative hypertensive crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ RET carriers → **prophylactic thyroidectomy** timed by variant risk; MEN2B generally in infancy
Genotype-directed surveillance for asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia: lifelong mild hypercalcemia with low urinary calcium
Marfan syndrome: ectopia lentis and aortic root dilation

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.evidence: Established MEN teaching; current surveillance guidance not checked online.

multiple-myeloma.name: Multiple myeloma
multiple-myeloma.scope: CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lytic lesions), SPEP/UPEP M-spike, serum free light chains, bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells), MGUS, smoldering myeloma
multiple-myeloma.core: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy causes monoclonal protein production and organ damage; modern biomarkers can establish treatment-requiring disease before symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, Black ancestry, male sex, preexisting MGUS; usually no identifiable preventable exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CRAB**: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, lytic bone lesions
Back/rib pain, pathologic fracture, recurrent bacterial infection, high total protein, rouleaux
Acute weakness/back pain → cord compression; proteinuria or restrictive cardiomyopathy → consider AL amyloid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow expansion suppresses blood formation; osteoclast activation without osteoblast response causes bone destruction
Light chains injure renal tubules; low polyclonal immunoglobulins → **encapsulated bacteria**, e.g., pneumococcus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **SPEP/immunofixation + free light chains**, urine studies; light-chain disease may lack serum spike
★ **Bone marrow biopsy** quantifies clonal plasma cells; whole-body low-dose CT/MRI assesses bone disease
Active disease: ≥10% clonal marrow cells/plasmacytoma plus attributable CRAB or myeloma-defining biomarker
SLiM: marrow ≥60%; involved/uninvolved FLC ratio ≥100 with involved FLC ≥100 mg/L
MRI >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm defines active disease; bone scan may miss lytic lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Bortezomib-based combination** ± daratumumab/lenalidomide/dexamethasone; selected patients → autologous transplant
Hypercalcemia → saline plus antiresorptive; AKI → hydration, avoid NSAIDs/contrast and rapidly reduce light chains
Cord compression → dexamethasone and urgent MRI/radiation or surgery; treat infections promptly
MGUS/smoldering disease generally monitored; high-risk smoldering disease merits specialist assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Cast nephropathy, vertebral collapse, hyperviscosity, AL amyloidosis; treatment-related neuropathy, infections and thrombosis
Urine dipstick detects albumin, misses light chains; negative dipstick does not exclude cast nephropathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccines, bisphosphonates; proteasome inhibitors → antiviral prophylaxis; immunomodulators → thromboprophylaxis by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metastatic carcinoma: destructive lesions without clonal plasma-cell findings
Waldenström macroglobulinemia: IgM, hyperviscosity/lymphadenopathy, usually no lytic lesions

multiple-myeloma.evidence: Criteria checked 2026-10-30: [IMWG diagnostic criteria](https://www.myeloma.org/newly-diagnosed/multiple-myeloma-diagnostic-criteria); treatment: established generalist teaching.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

myocarditis.name: Myocarditis
myocarditis.scope: Viral myocarditis, postviral heart failure, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, cardiac MRI, supportive heart failure therapy
myocarditis.core: New chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure after a viral syndrome raises concern for inflammatory myocardial injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent viral illness, autoimmune disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors and selected drug hypersensitivity
Chagas exposure and giant-cell/eosinophilic disorders matter in selected epidemiologic or fulminant presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitations; tachycardia disproportionate to fever
Troponin elevation, nonspecific ST–T abnormalities, ventricular ectopy; normal initial studies do not exclude
★ Syncope, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade AV block or shock → **high-risk myocarditis**
Concurrent pericarditis may produce pleuritic positional pain and diffuse ST elevation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct injury and immune-mediated inflammation damage cardiomyocytes → edema, necrosis and ventricular dysfunction
Residual scar creates an arrhythmic substrate even when systolic function improves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ECG, troponin, BNP and **echocardiography** assess injury, rhythm and function
★ **Cardiac MRI** identifies edema and nonischemic late gadolinium enhancement
Exclude ACS with coronary assessment when presentation/risk warrants; troponin alone cannot distinguish
Endomyocardial biopsy for selected fulminant, arrhythmic or unexplained progressive disease when etiology changes treatment
Routine broad viral serology rarely establishes myocardial cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable systolic HF → **diuresis and guideline-directed HF drugs**; defer beta blocker during shock
Hemodynamic compromise → ICU, vasopressors/inotropes and temporary mechanical circulatory support when refractory
Treat arrhythmias/AV block; pacing or defibrillation support when necessary
No routine steroids for presumed viral disease; giant-cell, eosinophilic and immune-mediated forms may need immunosuppression
Avoid NSAIDs for isolated myocarditis with HF; pericarditic pain requires individualized assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, persistent HF, ventricular tachycardia, sudden death and intracardiac thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Restrict strenuous exercise during active inflammation; return after symptom, imaging and rhythm reassessment
Classic restriction 3–6 months; newer guidance allows earlier individualized return in selected fully recovered athletes
Follow-up echo/MRI, ambulatory ECG and exercise testing guide clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: MI: coronary distribution ischemia/scar and culprit artery
Stress cardiomyopathy: characteristic reversible wall-motion pattern
Pericarditis alone: pericardial inflammation without myocardial dysfunction

necrotizing-enterocolitis.name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
necrotizing-enterocolitis.scope: Prematurity, formula feeding, abdominal distention, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, pneumoperitoneum, bowel rest, emergent exploratory laparotomy
necrotizing-enterocolitis.core: A vulnerable newborn develops feeding intolerance and systemic deterioration; intestinal wall gas establishes bowel injury requiring immediate medical and surgical evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Prematurity**, very low birth weight, formula feeding; human milk protective
Term infants: impaired intestinal perfusion from congenital heart disease or perinatal illness

rows.label: Clues
items: Abdominal distention, bilious residuals/emesis, hematochezia, reduced bowel sounds
Temperature instability, apnea, lethargy, bradycardia may precede obvious abdominal findings
★ Abdominal wall erythema/discoloration, peritonitis, shock → advanced disease
Thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, rising lactate support progression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature intestinal barrier + dysbiosis + inflammation → mucosal injury and bacterial invasion
Progressive necrosis may become transmural; bacterial gas enters bowel wall and portal circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Abdominal radiograph: **pneumatosis intestinalis**; portal venous gas supports diagnosis
Supine plus decubitus/cross-table imaging assesses free air; ultrasound evaluates perfusion and free fluid
CBC/platelets, electrolytes, blood gas/lactate, cultures; serial examinations and imaging track evolution
Early films may show only ileus; absence of pneumatosis does not exclude early NEC

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + NG/OG decompression**, IV fluids, cardiorespiratory support, early pediatric surgical consultation
IV ampicillin + gentamicin ± metronidazole for advanced disease; alternative: piperacillin-tazobactam
Parenteral nutrition during bowel rest; correct electrolyte disturbances, coagulopathy, anemia
★ **Pneumoperitoneum**, peritonitis, or deterioration despite treatment → emergency exploration and necrotic bowel resection
Extremely unstable infant: peritoneal drainage may temporize; reassess need for laparotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Sepsis, DIC, perforation, death; later intestinal strictures and obstruction
Extensive resection → short bowel syndrome, malabsorption, parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis
Growth impairment and neurodevelopmental disability among survivors

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Mother's milk or donor human milk; structured neonatal feeding protocols
Avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotics and acid suppression; routine probiotics lack universal US recommendation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spontaneous intestinal perforation: isolated perforation, often earlier, without diffuse pneumatosis
Malrotation/volvulus: sudden bilious emesis; urgent evaluation even with initially benign examination
Milk protein proctocolitis: bloody stools in otherwise well, growing infant

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

normal-and-abnormal-labor.name: Normal and abnormal labor
normal-and-abnormal-labor.scope: Latent vs active first stage, second stage, active phase protraction and arrest (oxytocin, cesarean), false labor (Braxton Hicks), operative vaginal delivery, labor induction
normal-and-abnormal-labor.core: True labor produces progressive cervical change; dystocia management depends on stage, contraction adequacy, fetal status, and descent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Nulliparity, obesity, fetal macrosomia, malposition, cephalopelvic disproportion, inadequate uterine contractions

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess membrane status, presentation, fetal heart tracing, serial dilation, station, and maternal vital signs
★ Tachysystole: **>5 contractions/10 minutes**, averaged over 30 minutes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysfunctional powers, passenger, or passage → delayed dilation or descent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active arrest requires ruptured membranes: no change after **4 hours adequate** or 6 hours inadequate contractions
Adequate: ≥200 Montevideo units (summed mm Hg/10 minutes); IUPC when external assessment insufficient
Prolonged pushing: >3 hours nulliparous, >2 hours multiparous; individualize by descent and fetal status
Failed induction requires ≥12–18 hours oxytocin after ROM; slow latent phase alone does not mandate cesarean
Presenting part unpalpable → **ultrasound** for lie/presentation before amniotomy; floating part → cord prolapse risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Protraction (<1 cm/2 hours) with weak contractions → **oxytocin**, amniotomy; established active arrest → cesarean
Tachysystole → stop oxytocin, lateral positioning; persistent fetal compromise → terbutaline, expedited delivery
★ Operative birth: full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, skilled operator; failed → cesarean
Unfavorable cervix → balloon or prostaglandin ripening, then oxytocin; avoid misoprostol after prior cesarean
Labor pain → **epidural** most effective first-stage; pudendal block covers second stage only

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal infection, hemorrhage, exhaustion; neonatal hypoxia
Forceps/vacuum → lacerations, scalp injury; vacuum → subgaleal hemorrhage, avoid <34 weeks or face presentation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Induce for maternal/fetal indications or offer elective induction from 39 weeks; no elective earlier delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: irregular, self-resolving, no cervical change → reassurance; GBS prophylaxis only in true labor/rupture
Obstructed labor: strong contractions, no progress; CPD (macrosomia), achondroplastic pelvis, transverse lie → **cesarean**, not oxytocin
Shoulder dystocia: head delivered, shoulders impacted; failed head descent at full dilation → CPD

table.title: Stages
rows: 6–10 cm; older exams may use ≥5 cm

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, secondary polycythemia or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance
Sleep-related hypoventilation with nocturnal hypercapnia → morning headaches

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Child adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy, even with pulmonary hypertension; selected adults → surgery, hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance
Awake postoperative hypercapnia → **CPAP/BiPAP**; reintubate only if obtunded or failing noninvasive support

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

occupational-lung-disease.name: Occupational lung disease
occupational-lung-disease.scope: Silicosis, asbestosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, berylliosis
occupational-lung-disease.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea and interstitial lung abnormalities years after dust exposure require a detailed occupational history and exposure-specific imaging interpretation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cumulative inhaled mineral dust, inadequate respiratory protection, mining/construction/manufacturing exposures
Long latency permits disease after retirement; smoking adds obstructive disease and cancer risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dry cough, exertional breathlessness, reduced exercise capacity; examination may show crackles
Advanced disease: resting hypoxemia, cyanosis, clubbing or right-heart strain
Pleural plaques mark exposure but often do not explain substantial functional impairment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Persistent particles activate macrophages and profibrotic pathways → irreversible interstitial scarring
Beryllium triggers a delayed cellular immune response with noncaseating granulomas

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Detailed job/task history + chest imaging**; HRCT clarifies radiograph findings
PFTs often restrictive with reduced DLCO; obstructive or mixed patterns can occur
★ Beryllium suspicion → **beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test**; biopsy may show granulomas
★ Silica exposure → **TB assessment**; evaluate fever, weight loss, cavitation for active infection
New unilateral pleural effusion, nodular pleural thickening, or mass → malignancy workup, tissue diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Stop further exposure**, smoking cessation; oxygen for hypoxemia, pulmonary rehabilitation
Vaccination and prompt infection treatment; bronchodilators if coexisting airflow obstruction
Symptomatic progressive berylliosis → systemic glucocorticoids; no proven reversal of established dust fibrosis
Advanced refractory respiratory failure → lung transplant evaluation; treat TB or cancer separately

rows.label: Complications
items: Progressive massive fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure
Asbestos: bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma; smoking synergizes lung carcinoma risk, not mesothelioma
Silicosis: TB/nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, lung cancer

rows.label: Prevention
items: Engineering dust controls, wet cutting, fitted respirators, occupational surveillance
Protect household contacts from contaminated work clothing; adherence to workplace exposure limits

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sarcoidosis: granulomas without relevant exposure; beryllium test negative
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: basal subpleural honeycombing without causative occupational history
Heart failure: congestion/effusions with cardiac dysfunction

occupational-lung-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established occupational pulmonary medicine teaching.

osteogenesis-imperfecta.name: Osteogenesis imperfecta
osteogenesis-imperfecta.scope: COL1A1 and COL1A2 mutations, type I collagen defect, multiple fractures, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, lethal perinatal type II
osteogenesis-imperfecta.core: Child with repeated low-impact injuries and extraosseous connective-tissue findings; variable skeletal severity can obscure the diagnosis or resemble nonaccidental trauma.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Usually **autosomal dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 variants**; family history or de novo mutation
Unaffected parents do not exclude disease; parental germline mosaicism may cause recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Multiple fractures with minimal trauma**, ligamentous laxity, easy bruising, bone deformity
**Dentinogenesis imperfecta**: opalescent, discolored teeth with early wear or breakage
Conductive/mixed hearing loss often develops later; normal intellect

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **Deficient or structurally abnormal type I collagen** impairs bone matrix and other collagen-rich tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: Skeletal radiographs: osteopenia, healed fractures, bowed bones, sometimes wormian skull bones
**Molecular genetic testing** confirms; skeletal survey assesses extent when clinically needed
Calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase usually normal outside fracture healing
Assess trauma consistency, full skin examination, family history; genetic disorder and abuse can coexist

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Fracture stabilization with **brief immobilization and early rehabilitation**; avoid prolonged disuse
IV pamidronate or zoledronic acid for significant skeletal disease → improved bone density
Recurrent fractures/deformity → intramedullary rodding; physical/occupational rehabilitation and mobility aids
Dental restoration, hearing aids, and orthopedic follow-up; adequate calcium/vitamin D without megadoses

rows.label: Complications
items: Scoliosis, restrictive lung disease, chronic pain, impaired mobility; cranial involvement → basilar invagination
Bisphosphonates: acute-phase reaction, hypocalcemia; coordinate major orthopedic procedures with bone specialist

rows.label: Prevention
items: Gentle handling, safe low-impact activity, fall prevention; weight-bearing within functional limits
Genetic counseling; prenatal testing when familial variant known; periodic dental and audiology assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonaccidental trauma: inconsistent history, patterned bruises, posterior rib/metaphyseal lesions; safeguarding evaluation
Rickets: growth-plate cupping/fraying, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Hypophosphatasia: low alkaline phosphatase, premature tooth loss

table.title: Classic phenotypes
rows: Prenatal fractures; perinatal lethality, respiratory failure

otitis-externa.name: Otitis externa
otitis-externa.scope: Acute diffuse otitis externa, swimmer ear prevention, topical fluoroquinolones, necrotizing otitis externa
otitis-externa.core: Otalgia worsened by moving the pinna or pressing the tragus, with an inflamed external canal, indicates otitis externa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Swimming, moisture, canal trauma from cotton swabs/hearing aids, eczema
Diabetes, older age, immunosuppression → necrotizing infection risk; Pseudomonas often responsible

rows.label: Clues
items: Canal erythema, edema, debris, otorrhea; conductive hearing loss from occlusion
★ **Severe nocturnal pain disproportionate to examination**, granulation tissue → necrotizing otitis externa
Facial weakness or other cranial neuropathy suggests skull-base extension; fever may be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of acidic cerumen barrier permits bacterial proliferation; typical organisms Pseudomonas and S aureus
Necrotizing form invades soft tissue and skull base rather than remaining superficial

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy + tragal/pinna tenderness**; inspect tympanic membrane when visible
Routine uncomplicated cases require no culture or imaging; refractory infection → culture, assess fungal/dermatologic causes
★ Suspected invasive disease → **ESR/CRP, culture, CT temporal bone ± MRI**
Biopsy suspicious persistent granulation to exclude malignancy; MRI better defines soft tissue/cranial involvement

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated → **topical ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin ± steroid**, usually 7–10 days
Gentle canal cleaning; marked edema → wick to deliver drops; acetaminophen/NSAID for pain
Known/suspected perforation or tubes → nonototoxic fluoroquinolone; avoid aminoglycoside/alcohol drops
No routine oral antibiotic unless extension beyond canal, high-risk host, or inability to deliver topical treatment
★ Necrotizing infection → **urgent ENT + systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics**, often prolonged, culture-directed

rows.label: Complications
items: Periauricular cellulitis, canal stenosis, skull-base osteomyelitis, cranial neuropathy
Persistent pain despite drops → reassess technique, obstruction, wrong organism, invasive disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Keep ear dry during treatment; avoid canal instrumentation and cotton swabs
Recurrent → dry externally, **alcohol-acetic acid drops** after swimming; only with intact membrane, no tubes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute otitis media: middle-ear effusion/bulging TM, little tragal tenderness
Otomycosis: prominent itching, fungal debris, antibiotic-drop history
Mastoiditis: postauricular swelling/tenderness and protruding pinna

otitis-externa.evidence: Not checked online; established otolaryngology topical treatment and invasive-infection principles.

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea permissible despite risks; reassess sedation/respiration
Codeine fails → morphine/oxycodone; pain mimics depression; wears off early → shorten interval

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids**, short-acting for breakthrough; constipation → keep dose, add stimulant laxative

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals
Advanced dementia refusing intake → comfort hand-feeding by mouth; no tubes or IV

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Hospice: unrelated conditions remain treatable; no DNR requirement; enrollment revocable if goals change
Cancer pain: escalating requests → tolerance/progression, not addiction; past OUD never limits analgesia

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

table.title: Care settings
rows: Adjust with hospice team; avoid readmission

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones (prior postprandial biliary colic), heavy alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease
Blunt abdominal trauma + epigastric mass/raised enzymes → contrast CT for pancreatic/duodenal injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue: ↓insulin, ↓glucagon, normal insulin sensitivity; lipase may normalize

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase or amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT: diagnostic doubt, high fever/marked leukocytosis (necrosis?), deterioration, no improvement by 48–72 hours; not routine early
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency
Recurrent, no gallstones/alcohol → EUS or MRCP for ductal anatomy; older exam questions may expect ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, reassessment, IV opioid analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** by 48 hours if tolerated; else enteral; older exam questions may expect initial bowel rest
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Uncomplicated/sterile: no antibiotics; infected necrosis: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancrelipase, fat-soluble vitamins, pain control; islet-loss diabetes → **insulin**, not sulfonylureas

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; necrosis, hemorrhage; **splenic vein thrombosis** → isolated gastric varices, normal liver
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

pituitary-adenomas.name: Pituitary adenomas
pituitary-adenomas.scope: Prolactinoma, acromegaly, nonfunctioning adenoma, pituitary apoplexy
pituitary-adenomas.core: Pituitary tumors cause hormone excess, pituitary failure, or sellar mass effects; determine functional status before choosing medical treatment or surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most sporadic; MEN1 with associated parathyroid/pancreatic endocrine tumors
Apoplexy may follow tumor hemorrhage/infarction, anticoagulation, pregnancy or major physiologic stress

rows.label: Clues
items: Mass effect → headache and bitemporal hemianopia from optic-chiasm compression
Pituitary failure → fatigue, hypotension, low libido; prolactin-related gonadal suppression may cause infertility
★ **Sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, hypotension** → pituitary apoplexy
GH excess may cause macroglossia, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet and worsening ring/shoe size

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autonomous secretion causes hormone excess; stalk compression interrupts dopamine inhibition, modestly raising prolactin
Expanding sellar tissue compresses normal pituitary and optic pathways; acute infarction can eliminate ACTH reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hormonal assessment → **contrast pituitary MRI**; formal visual fields if lesion abuts chiasm
Check prolactin, IGF-1, AM cortisol, free T4/TSH and gonadal axis; screen cortisol excess when clinically suspected
Elevated prolactin → exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and dopamine-blocking drugs
Large mass with unexpectedly modest prolactin → dilute assay for **hook effect**
Acromegaly: elevated age-adjusted IGF-1 → failure of GH suppression after oral glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected apoplexy → **IV hydrocortisone immediately**, fluids, urgent MRI and neurosurgical/endocrine assessment
Persistent severe visual deficits or reduced consciousness → urgent decompression after stabilization
★ Replace glucocorticoids **before levothyroxine** when both axes deficient
Prolactinoma → **cabergoline**, even with visual deficits; older exam questions may expect bromocriptine
Residual GH excess after surgery → octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant; radiation for selected refractory tumors

rows.label: Complications
items: Visual loss, adrenal crisis, hypogonadism; surgery → CSF leak, diabetes insipidus or panhypopituitarism
Acromegaly → cardiomyopathy, diabetes, sleep apnea, colon neoplasia; cabergoline → nausea/orthostasis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Craniopharyngioma: suprasellar cystic/calcified lesion, often childhood onset
Primary hypothyroidism: ↑TSH/↓free T4 with secondary prolactin elevation; medication effect: no autonomous tumor secretion

pituitary-adenomas.evidence: Prolactinoma checked 2026-10-30: [Pituitary Society consensus, 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-023-00886-5); other sellar emergencies: established teaching.

table.title: Subtype-directed management
rows: Observe if small; surgery for compression

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced fremitus; large effusion shifts mediastinum away; unilateral + cancer history → malignant
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid/empyema
Bloody fluid: malignancy (prior cancer, mediastinal mass), embolism, trauma; milky → chyle
Foul-smelling pus after aspiration → **anaerobic empyema**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage
Heart-failure transudate: pleural protein <3 g/dL, low LDH and cell count; **glucose equals serum**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, **pH <7.20** or glucose <60 → empyema/complicated: chest tube, antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.name: Population health and quality improvement
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.scope: Program evaluation, outcome and process measures, health equity, PDSA cycles
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.core: Improve care for a defined population through measurable aims, iterative system changes, and attention to unequal access and outcomes.

rows.label: Principle
items: Population denominator includes eligible people missing visits, not only those receiving care
Equity: stratify outcomes by language, race/ethnicity, geography, disability, insurance, deprivation
Greater relative **primary care investment** improves population health, reduces disparities

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Define **measurable aim**, population, baseline, timeframe; engage patients/frontline staff
★ **PDSA**: plan small change → do → study results → act/adapt before scaling
Stratify measures, address interpreter/transport/cost barriers, monitor unintended consequences

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not assume a favorable outcome proves causation without comparison and context
Avoid blaming individuals for failures created by unreliable workflows

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Run/control charts distinguish routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals over time
Program evaluation: reach, fidelity, effectiveness, cost, sustainability versus original goals
Education program → measure knowledge/behavior change; small cohort cannot detect morbidity/mortality

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Process success ≠ patient benefit**; assess both and choose valid denominators
★ **Risk adjustment** improves comparison; also report disparities so adjustment cannot conceal inequity
Before–after improvement may reflect secular trends, case-mix change, regression to mean

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.evidence: Established quality-improvement and program-evaluation principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

prion-disease.name: Prion disease
prion-disease.scope: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sporadic, familial, variant), rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus, ataxia, 14-3-3 protein, RT-QuIC, periodic sharp wave complexes, spongiform encephalopathy
prion-disease.core: Cognitive decline over weeks to months with stimulus-sensitive jerks and cerebellar dysfunction suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sporadic CJD usually older adults; familial cases involve autosomal dominant PRNP variants
Iatrogenic: contaminated neurosurgical equipment/tissue; variant CJD: bovine spongiform encephalopathy-contaminated beef

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Rapid progression** to akinetic mutism; visual, pyramidal, or extrapyramidal abnormalities
Startle myoclonus often develops after initial behavioral or memory changes
Variant CJD: younger age, early psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory complaints; prolonged course

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Misfolded protein templates conversion of normal prion protein; no nucleic acid
Neuronal loss, gliosis and vacuolation → spongiform encephalopathy without prominent inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Brain **MRI DWI**: cortical ribboning and caudate/putamen diffusion restriction
★ CSF **RT-QuIC** detects abnormal prion seeding; high specificity
CSF 14-3-3 reflects rapid neuronal injury; supportive but nonspecific
EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes; absence does not exclude disease
Exclude treatable mimics: CSF inflammatory/infectious studies, metabolic testing, autoimmune evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive/palliative care**; no established disease-modifying treatment
Clonazepam or levetiracetam for distressing myoclonus; nutrition and caregiver support
Brain biopsy rarely needed; notify infection control before invasive tissue procedures

rows.label: Complications
items: Dysphagia, aspiration, immobility; sporadic CJD usually fatal within one year

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prion-specific instrument decontamination or disposal; routine sterilization insufficient
Familial disease → genetic counseling; casual contact does not transmit CJD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autoimmune encephalitis: seizures, inflammatory findings; potentially immunotherapy-responsive
Alzheimer disease: progression over years
Wernicke encephalopathy: malnutrition, ophthalmoplegia; treat promptly with IV thiamine

prion-disease.evidence: Diagnosis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC CJD overview](https://www.cdc.gov/creutzfeldt-jakob/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); established supportive care.

pubertal-development.name: Pubertal development
pubertal-development.scope: Tanner stages, normal thelarche vs breast mass, premature adrenarche, precocious puberty, constitutional delay of growth and puberty
pubertal-development.core: Interpret sexual maturation by sequence, age, growth velocity, and bone age; isolated benign variants lack progressive gonadal activation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constitutional delay often familial; chronic illness, undernutrition, excess exercise delay maturation
CNS lesions, gonadal/adrenal hormone excess, exogenous sex steroids can cause early puberty

rows.label: Clues
items: Girls: breast budding precedes peak growth, then menarche about 2–3 years later
Boys: testes enlarge before penile growth; pubic hair reflects adrenarche, not necessarily gonadarche
★ Asymmetric tender **subareolar breast bud** at expected age usually normal; hard eccentric mass needs evaluation
Rapid height acceleration, advancing secondary characteristics, neurologic symptoms → pathologic early maturation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central puberty: hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility → LH/FSH → gonadal steroids
Adrenarche produces adrenal androgens independently; peripheral hormone excess suppresses pituitary gonadotropins
Immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis → irregular anovulatory cycles, normal for 2–3 years after menarche
Virilized boy with **prepubertal testes** → peripheral androgen, usually adrenal; central puberty enlarges testes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Precocious: secondary sexual development **before 8 years girls or 9 years boys**
★ Delayed: **no breasts by 13**, no testes ≥4 mL by 14; evaluate absent menarche by 15
Growth chart, Tanner examination, bone age; LH/FSH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH selected by pattern
Central precocity → pubertal basal/stimulated LH; brain MRI especially boys, young girls, neurologic signs
Peripheral pattern → targeted adrenal/gonadal tests/imaging; isolated adrenarche requires exclusion of rapid virilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Progressive central precocity → **GnRH agonist**; treat CNS cause when present
Peripheral precocity → remove hormone source or treat tumor/adrenal disorder; GnRH agonist alone ineffective
Constitutional delay → reassurance, follow growth; distress → specialist-guided brief sex-steroid course
Benign premature thelarche/adrenarche → observe progression; no automatic hormonal treatment
Pubertal gynecomastia, unilateral or bilateral, smooth subareolar → **reassurance**; no labs/biopsy; carcinoma very rare

rows.label: Complications
items: Early epiphyseal closure → reduced adult height; psychosocial distress
Missed hypogonadism → impaired bone accrual; untreated CNS/tumor cause may progress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, manage chronic disease, avoid household hormone exposure; serial growth surveillance
Normal puberty + moodiness, mild parent conflict → **puberty education** for child, parents; no drug testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary gonadal failure: high LH/FSH, low sex steroids
Permanent central hypogonadism: absent progression rather than eventual familial catch-up
Familial short stature: short parents, bone age matches chronologic age; constitutional delay: **delayed bone age**

table.title: Tanner staging anchors
rows: Further enlargement; menarche usually within 1–2 years

pubertal-development.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric endocrine timing and Tanner staging.

renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.name: Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors
renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.scope: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, direct renin inhibitors, hyperkalemia, angioedema, cough
renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.core: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aliskiren interrupt the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis at different steps.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ **ACE inhibitor or ARB**: hypertension with albuminuric CKD; post-MI ventricular dysfunction
HFrEF: ACE inhibitor/ARB when sacubitril-valsartan cannot be used; aliskiren lacks outcome benefits

rows.label: Mechanism
items: ACE cleaves **C-terminal dipeptide** of angiotensin I → angiotensin II; inhibitors block this step
Efferent arteriolar dilation → ↓glomerular filtration pressure; ↓aldosterone → potassium retention

rows.label: Adverse
items: Hypotension, AKI during hypovolemia; modest stable creatinine rise expected
★ **Angioedema → stop ACE inhibitor permanently**, assess/protect airway; possible even after years

rows.label: Avoid
items: ★ **Pregnancy**, bilateral renal artery stenosis, uncontrolled hyperkalemia
Prior ACE angioedema → no ACE inhibitor; subsequent ARB needs individualized assessment

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ **Never combine ACE inhibitor, ARB, or aliskiren**; additive kidney injury and hyperkalemia
Potassium supplements, spironolactone, trimethoprim → ↑K; NSAID + diuretic → AKI
Sacubitril-valsartan requires **36-hour ACE inhibitor washout**; RAAS blockade can raise lithium

rows.label: Monitor
items: Baseline BP, creatinine, K → repeat within **2–4 weeks** after initiation/dose increase
Creatinine rise >30% → investigate volume depletion, NSAIDs, renovascular disease; reassess drug

rows.label: Traps
items: Advanced CKD alone → no automatic discontinuation; manage reversible hyperkalemia contributors first

research-ethics.name: Research ethics
research-ethics.scope: Institutional review board (IRB), vulnerable populations (prisoners, children), coercion and undue inducement, clinical equipoise, informed consent in research
research-ethics.core: Scientifically valid research requires independent oversight, fair selection, favorable risk-benefit balance, and voluntary informed participation with additional safeguards for vulnerability.

rows.label: Principle
items: Respect for persons, beneficence, justice: autonomy, minimize harm, equitable recruitment
★ **Clinical equipoise**: expert uncertainty about superior treatment; personal doubt insufficient
Vulnerability warrants safeguards, not automatic exclusion from scientifically justified studies

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **IRB approval before recruitment**; disclose conflicts, monitor harms, report unexpected problems
Explain purpose, randomization, risks, uncertain benefits, alternatives, privacy, injury care, contacts
★ **Ongoing consent**: check understanding, answer questions, update risks; withdrawal without penalty

rows.label: Don't
items: Coercion: threaten lost care, employment, grades, liberty for refusal; parole offer to prisoners
Undue influence: incentives distort voluntary judgment; reasonable reimbursement/payment permitted
Placebo causing serious harm by withholding proven care; disguise research as personalized treatment

rows.label: Exceptions
items: IRB waiver: minimal risk, impracticable otherwise, preserved rights/welfare; later disclosure when needed
Identifiable-data waiver: study also impracticable without identifiers
Emergency research: prior regulatory safeguards/approval; treatment emergency exception insufficient

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **IRB approval never replaces informed consent** unless an authorized waiver applies
Capable child's dissent generally respected despite parental permission
Therapeutic misconception: participant assumes every study decision maximizes personal clinical benefit

table.title: Additional safeguards
rows: Parental permission plus developmentally capable child's assent
Permitted research category; prisoner representative on IRB
Legally authorized representative; seek participant assent

rickets.name: Rickets
rickets.scope: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency, X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, metaphyseal cupping and fraying, elevated alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate, high PTH
rickets.core: Growing child with bowed legs, widened wrists, and delayed growth: evaluate defective growth-plate mineralization rather than treating the deformity alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Nutritional: **unsupplemented breastfeeding**, low dietary calcium, limited sunlight, darker skin, malabsorption
Inherited phosphate wasting: X-linked dominant; affected fathers transmit to all daughters, no sons

rows.label: Clues
items: Rachitic rosary, craniotabes, delayed fontanelle closure, bone pain, hypotonia, delayed walking
Hypocalcemic tetany, seizures, prolonged QT, cardiomyopathy → urgent stabilization
Persistent short stature, lower-limb deformity, dental abscesses despite adequate vitamin D → phosphate-wasting disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nutritional deficiency → reduced intestinal calcium absorption → secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal phosphate loss
**PHEX mutation → excess FGF23**, renal phosphaturia and inappropriately low calcitriol

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Wrist/knee radiograph → **metaphyseal cupping, fraying, widened growth plates**
★ Check **calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D**, creatinine; ALP elevated, phosphate reduced
25-OH vitamin D <12 ng/mL supports deficiency; interpret with calcium intake and biochemical pattern
Normal vitamin D with hypophosphatemia → assess renal phosphate wasting; genetic evaluation if inherited pattern

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic hypocalcemia → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**, then oral calcium
During repletion → repeat calcium/phosphate/ALP; assess radiographic healing
Burosumab must not accompany oral phosphate/active vitamin D; specialist monitoring prevents excess phosphate
Persistent renal disease/acidosis → treat cause; orthopedic correction only for residual deformity after metabolic control

rows.label: Complications
items: Fractures, permanent deformity, impaired growth; severe hypocalcemia → arrhythmia
Phosphate/calcitriol: ↑PTH, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis → urine calcium and renal ultrasound monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Infants: **vitamin D 400 IU/day**; after 12 months, total intake 600 IU/day plus calcium-rich foods
Maternal nutrition, supplementation during malabsorption, and family counseling for inherited disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic bowing: symmetric toddler legs, normal growth plates/laboratory studies
Blount disease: focal medial tibial growth disturbance, often obesity; normal mineral studies
Osteogenesis imperfecta: fragile collagen, blue sclerae; no characteristic growth-plate changes

routine-prenatal-care.name: Routine prenatal care and early pregnancy
routine-prenatal-care.scope: Pregnancy diagnosis (beta-hCG), initial prenatal assessment, routine first-trimester screening, aneuploidy screening
routine-prenatal-care.core: Confirm and date pregnancy, assess maternal risks, offer one aneuploidy-screening strategy or diagnostic testing, and arrange time-sensitive prenatal studies.

rows.label: Who
items: All pregnancies; review obstetric history, drugs, illness, substance use, violence, family history
Offer carrier screening and genetic counseling; discuss patient preferences and right to decline

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Early visit: urine hCG confirms pregnancy; serum quantitative hCG for uncertain/complicated cases
★ First-trimester **ultrasound crown–rump length** best establishes gestational age
Serum screen 10–13 6/7 weeks; NT 11–13 6/7; cfDNA from 10 weeks

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Initial **CBC, ABO/Rh, antibody screen, urine culture**; HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, HCV, rubella immunity
GC/chlamydia by age/risk; offer one aneuploidy strategy regardless of maternal age
Anatomy ultrasound 18–22 weeks; AFP for open neural tube defects when not otherwise assessed

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Abnormal screen → counseling, ultrasound, **CVS/amniocentesis** before irreversible decisions
CVS: 10–13 weeks; amniocentesis: ≥15 weeks; neither automatically required after negative screening
Rh-negative, unsensitized → anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks and after sensitizing events

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **cfDNA is screening**, not diagnostic; does not screen open neural tube defects
Single hCG value cannot establish viability or location; pain/bleeding → ectopic evaluation
Folate before conception/early gestation; avoid alcohol, tobacco, teratogens; no live vaccines

table.title: Early and routine pregnancy calls
rows: Nausea, irregular bleeding or amenorrhea, even premenarche
Missed menses, urinary frequency, friable cervix, enlarged uterus
Brief sharp movement-triggered lower-quadrant pain, normal vitals
No added preterm, fluid, or placental risk

sarcoidosis.name: Sarcoidosis
sarcoidosis.scope: Noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, hypercalcemia, extrapulmonary manifestations (uveitis, erythema nodosum, neurosarcoidosis, cardiac), systemic corticosteroids
sarcoidosis.core: Multisystem granulomatous disease, classically a young adult with bilateral hilar adenopathy; treat threatened organ function rather than an abnormal radiograph alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young or middle-aged adults; higher prevalence and disease burden among Black Americans
Familial predisposition; environmental antigen exposure suspected, without one established infectious cause

rows.label: Clues
items: Dry cough, exertional dyspnea; restrictive physiology and ↓DLCO; upper-lung interstitial infiltrates
★ **Löfgren syndrome**: erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + hilar adenopathy; usually favorable prognosis
Uveitis, lupus pernio, parotid enlargement; facial palsy, hypothalamic dysfunction suggest neurosarcoidosis
★ Unexplained **AV block, ventricular arrhythmia, syncope** → cardiac involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CD4-mediated granulomas; macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria, suppressed PTH

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Chest radiograph**, PFTs; baseline calcium, creatinine, liver tests, ECG and eye examination
Compatible presentation + **noncaseating granulomas** + exclusion of TB/fungi/beryllium exposure
Sample accessible lesion or EBUS-guided hilar/mediastinal node; classic Löfgren presentation may avoid biopsy
ACE level neither sensitive nor specific; cardiac symptoms/ECG abnormalities → cardiac MRI ± FDG-PET

rows.label: Tx
items: Asymptomatic stage I disease, preserved function → observation with clinical/PFT follow-up
★ **Prednisone** for progressive symptomatic pulmonary disease, significant hypercalcemia, cardiac or neurologic disease
Uveitis → urgent ophthalmology, topical or systemic corticosteroids according to severity
Steroid-dependent disease → methotrexate; refractory organ-threatening disease → specialist-directed infliximab
Hypercalcemia → hydration; restrict excess calcium/vitamin D and sunlight exposure

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, respiratory failure; nephrolithiasis and kidney injury
Cardiomyopathy, sudden death; visual loss; chronic steroids → infection, osteoporosis, diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prevention; smoking cessation and vaccination reduce respiratory morbidity
Monitor treatment toxicity and bone health; individualize vitamin D replacement because calcitriol may already be elevated

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal infection: organisms or positive microbiology; exclude before immunosuppression
Berylliosis: aerospace/industrial exposure, positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test
Lymphoma: malignant tissue, constitutional symptoms; granulomas alone do not exclude concurrent cancer

schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.name: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.scope: Brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, mesolimbic dopamine
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.core: Psychosis with impaired reality testing: distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders by duration, functional decline, and the relationship between mood episodes and psychosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, neurodevelopmental vulnerability; adolescent cannabis exposure increases risk
Typical onset late adolescence/early adulthood; exclude stimulant, hallucinogen, medication, and neurologic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior; negative symptoms: avolition, alogia, flat affect
★ At least **two core symptoms**, including delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, for active-phase diagnosis
Suicidality, dangerous commands or inability to eat → urgent safety assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **↑Mesolimbic dopamine** → positive symptoms; mesocortical → negative symptoms, early working-memory deficits
D2 blockade reduces psychosis but nigrostriatal/tuberoinfundibular effects cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia
Structural correlate: **enlarged lateral and third ventricles**, reduced cortical volume

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical history, collateral information, mental status; assess mood timeline and substance exposure
First episode → CBC/CMP, TSH, toxicology; HIV/syphilis or neuroimaging for relevant risks/atypical neurologic findings
★ **Schizoaffective**: ≥2 weeks psychosis without mood episode; mood episodes occupy most illness duration

rows.label: Tx
items: Safety crisis → hospitalization; acute agitation → de-escalation, then medication if needed
★ **Risperidone, aripiprazole or olanzapine** + coordinated specialty care, family education, CBT, supported employment
Schizoaffective depressive/bipolar subtype → add antidepressant or mood stabilizer according to mood syndrome
★ Failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials or persistent substantial suicide risk → **clozapine**
Adherence difficulty → long-acting injectable (haloperidol decanoate); catatonia → lorazepam, then ECT if refractory

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, homelessness, substance use, cardiometabolic disease; antipsychotics → metabolic syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, NMS
Clozapine → neutropenia, myocarditis, severe constipation; monitor ANC and symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid cannabis/stimulants; maintenance medication, relapse planning reduce recurrence
Monitor weight, BP, glucose, lipids; address tobacco use and cardiovascular risk
**High expressed emotion** (family criticism, hostility) → relapse; family therapy reduces recurrence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mood disorder with psychosis: psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes
Delirium: fluctuating attention/awareness and acute medical cause
Delusional disorder: ≥1 month delusions with otherwise relatively preserved function, limited other psychotic symptoms
Substance/medication-induced psychosis: recent stimulants (mydriasis, tremor) or corticosteroids, intact orientation

secondary-hypertension.name: Secondary hypertension
secondary-hypertension.scope: Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, diagnostic workup
secondary-hypertension.core: Abrupt, unusually young, severe, or resistant hypertension suggests a treatable secondary driver.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Renal stenosis: older smoker → atherosclerotic **lipid plaque**; young/middle-aged woman → **fibromuscular dysplasia** (medial hyperplasia, renal + carotid)
Renal disease, adrenal tumors, sleep apnea
NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, stimulants, glucocorticoids, licorice; medication nonadherence can mimic resistance

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis** → aldosterone excess, primary or renovascular; normal K does not exclude it
**Abdominal bruit**, diffuse atherosclerosis, late abrupt worsening, small unilateral kidney → renal artery stenosis
Flash pulmonary edema or creatinine rise >30% after ACE inhibitor/ARB → renovascular disease
**Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations** → pheochromocytoma; cushingoid appearance, upper-body hypertension guide testing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Renal hypoperfusion → juxtaglomerular **renin** → RAAS; ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction → ↓renal flow, ↓GFR across stenosis
Autonomous aldosterone → distal sodium absorption, potassium loss, low renin; pressure natriuresis escape prevents edema
Adrenal medullary catecholamine or cortisol excess, aortic obstruction, or nocturnal hypoxia increases vascular pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **home/ambulatory BP**, adherence, cuff technique; BMP, urinalysis, creatinine, TSH
Sleep-apnea symptoms → polysomnography; abnormal urinary sediment → renal ultrasound and kidney evaluation
★ Biochemical testing precedes adrenal imaging; correct hypokalemia and account for interfering medications
Endocrine Society 2025: suggest **aldosterone screening for all hypertension**, conditional on resources

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Primary aldosteronism: unilateral → **adrenalectomy**; bilateral → spironolactone/eplerenone
Renovascular atherosclerosis → medical risk reduction; revascularize selected recurrent pulmonary edema or refractory disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia → angioplasty; critical bilateral renal stenosis → avoid ACE inhibitor/ARB
★ Pheochromocytoma: **alpha blockade before beta blockade**, volume expansion, then surgery
Treat cortisol source, repair significant coarctation, use CPAP for OSA; stop contributing drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can cause catecholamine crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor renal function/K after RAAS blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists
Genetic evaluation/family screening for suspected hereditary pheochromocytoma or congenital aortic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: normal out-of-office readings
Essential hypertension: gradual course without specific endocrine/renal clues

table.title: Targeted workup
rows: Selective suppression test; CT/adrenal venous sampling
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines

secondary-hypertension.evidence: Aldosterone screening checked 2026-10-30: [Endocrine Society 2025](https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2); other causes: established teaching.

septic-arthritis.name: Septic arthritis
septic-arthritis.scope: Nongonococcal, gonococcal, prosthetic joint infection, IV drug use, empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime), contiguous osteomyelitis
septic-arthritis.core: Acutely painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion → urgent aspiration and drainage; delayed treatment rapidly destroys cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthesis, recent surgery/injection, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteremia
IV drug use → S aureus and gram-negative risk, including Pseudomonas
Young sexually active adults → disseminated gonorrhea; adjacent ulcers/osteomyelitis → contiguous spread
RA joint with new febrile monoarthritis → infection until aspirated, not flare

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually acute monoarthritis, often knee; fever may be absent, especially in older/immunocompromised adults
★ **Severe pain with both active and passive motion**; inability to bear weight; child's hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated
Gonococcal dissemination: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules; may progress to purulent monoarthritis
Prosthetic infection: persistent pain, loosening, wound drainage or sinus tract, sometimes minimal systemic illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation → neutrophilic enzymes damage articular cartilage
Implant biofilm limits antibiotic eradication without surgical source control
★ **S aureus** most common, including RA-damaged joints: gram-positive cocci in clusters
Asplenia or recent pharyngitis → **streptococci**: gram-positive cocci in chains

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Arthrocentesis before antibiotics** when stable: cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Synovial WBC >50,000/µL, neutrophil predominance supports infection; lower counts or negative Gram stain never exclude
★ **Crystals do not exclude infection**; send cultures even when gout seems likely
Blood cultures; gonococcal: aspirate on **chocolate/Thayer-Martin agar** plus mucosal NAAT; MRI for suspected contiguous osteomyelitis
New warmth/effusion in OA joint → aspirate before any intra-articular steroid

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ After cultures → **IV vancomycin + cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam** for severe disease, IV drug use, gram-negative risk
Stable low-risk adult: vancomycin ± ceftriaxone based on exposure; narrow to organism/susceptibility
