Sepsis → immediate antibiotics without delaying for aspiration; large joints: arthroscopic washout; **hip → operative drainage**, not serial aspiration
Persistent symptoms → repeat drainage, seek abscess/osteomyelitis; mobilize after infection controlled

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible joint destruction, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, sepsis
Prolonged antibiotics → renal injury, line complications, C difficile; prolonged immobility → stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sterile procedures, treat skin infections, injection-harm reduction
Gonorrhea: treat partners, screen other STIs, abstain until treatment completed and partners treated

rows.label: Mimics
items: Crystal arthritis: polarized crystals; infection still possible concurrently
Bursitis: localized periarticular swelling, passive joint motion relatively preserved
Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory arthritis after GI/GU infection
Transient synovitis (child): afebrile, bears weight, ESR <40, WBC <12,000

table.title: Special treatment branches
rows: Debridement, implant retention, prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk
Procedure bleeding: thoracentesis → intercostal artery, hemothorax; splenectomy → hemoperitoneum, left shoulder pain

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: **lost sympathetic tone** → hypotension, bradycardia or no tachycardia, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid
Warm sepsis: high output, **high mixed venous O2**; pump failure: low contractility, congestion; hypovolemia: low preload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
**Serial lactate**: hypoperfusion, best predicts course and mortality; trend with capillary refill, urine output
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation
CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, IV access; **isotonic crystalloid** (balanced, 0.9% saline) before imaging; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + blood products** (emergency O-negative); crystalloid as bridge; no vasopressors
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone
Pulmonary edema after fluids → stop boluses, **inotrope**; children: epinephrine preferred, older exams may expect dopamine

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose
Isolated head injury: hypertension + bradycardia (Cushing); trauma hypotension + tachycardia → assume hemorrhage

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

sickle-cell-disease.name: Sickle cell disease
sickle-cell-disease.scope: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, stroke, sickle cell trait, hemoglobin electrophoresis
sickle-cell-disease.core: HbS polymerization causes chronic hemolysis and episodic vascular occlusion; fever, hypoxemia and focal neurologic deficits require urgent escalation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive β-globin disease; dehydration, hypoxemia, cold and infection trigger sickling
Functional asplenia → encapsulated infection from early childhood; **S. pneumoniae** leads pneumonia and fulminant sepsis

rows.label: Clues
items: Baseline anemia, reticulocytosis, jaundice; childhood dactylitis or recurrent severe bone pain
Acute chest syndrome: **new pulmonary infiltrate** plus fever, respiratory symptoms or hypoxemia
Sequestration: sudden splenomegaly, falling hemoglobin, shock; aplasia: **low reticulocyte count**, often parvovirus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes → rigid erythrocytes, endothelial injury, ischemia and shortened RBC survival
Acute chest trigger: **infection** most common; in situ thrombosis and fat embolism less often
Severe anemia → low viscosity, vasodilation, ↓afterload → **↑cardiac output** preserves oxygen delivery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC confirms genotype; newborn screen detects disease before symptoms
Crisis → CBC, reticulocytes, bilirubin; fever → blood cultures; respiratory symptoms → chest radiograph
New focal deficit → emergency brain imaging, without delaying transfusion preparation
Distinguish osteomyelitis from infarction using cultures and MRI when focal fever/pain persists

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain crisis → prompt **IV opioid**, morphine (AKI: lower dose or hydromorphone); no meperidine; NSAID only if kidneys normal
Pain crisis support: euvolemic hydration; oxygen only for hypoxemia; no routine transfusion
★ Acute chest → oxygen, **ceftriaxone + azithromycin**, incentive spirometry; transfuse for significant anemia
Severe acute chest, stroke → **urgent exchange transfusion**; sequestration (cautious) or aplasia → simple transfusion
Fever → immediate **IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime**, despite daily penicillin prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, avascular necrosis, priapism, pigment gallstones, nephropathy, retinopathy
Repeated transfusions → alloimmunization and iron overload; delayed hyperhemolysis can worsen anemia
Chronic hemolysis → ↑folate demand → **folate deficiency**, macrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hydroxyurea** raises HbF, reduces crises; monitor CBC
Penicillin prophylaxis through age 5 in HbSS; pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib and influenza vaccines
Annual transcranial Doppler ages 2–16 in HbSS/HbSβ0; abnormal → chronic transfusion program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: persistent localized pain, fever; Salmonella or S. aureus
Iron deficiency: low ferritin, no hemolytic pattern

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal infection, especially diabetes → Fournier gangrene/necrotizing fasciitis; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal, S aureus possible; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread, toxins → necrosis, sepsis; minor trauma, no crepitus → **GAS**; crepitus → Clostridium/polymicrobial
Tinea pedis = portal of entry: acute fever/cellulitis is bacterial (S aureus/streptococcal) superinfection, not Trichophyton

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Moderate cellulitis (systemic signs) → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk or cephalexin failure → vancomycin; severe → + pip-tazo
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage
Pregnancy + suspected MRSA → clindamycin or vancomycin; **no doxycycline or fluoroquinolones**

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash
Superficial thrombophlebitis: palpable indurated venous cord, not lymphatic streaks

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed
Tender red streaks from skin break toward nodes
Usually S pyogenes; cephalexin; IV if systemic
Itchy follicular pustules on trunk/thighs after hot tub

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established IDSA-based infection management.

skin-cancer.name: Skin cancer
skin-cancer.scope: Actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, photoprotection and sunscreen
skin-cancer.core: Changing pigmented lesions or persistent keratinizing, pearly, or ulcerated growths require examination and tissue diagnosis rather than empiric reassurance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: UV exposure, fair skin, sunburns, tanning beds, older age; immunosuppression particularly increases SCC
Melanoma: numerous/atypical nevi, family/personal melanoma history; may arise without a preexisting nevus
Chronic wounds/scars predispose SCC; acral melanoma occurs regardless of skin pigmentation

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Melanoma: **ABCDE**—asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter, evolution; ugly-duckling lesion
Diameter >6 mm concerning, but smaller evolving lesions still require biopsy
Amelanotic melanoma may be pink; inspect soles, palms, nail beds; nail pigment extending onto fold concerning
Rapid growth, bleeding, nonhealing ulcer, fixation, neurologic symptoms, nodes → aggressive or advanced disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: UV-induced DNA damage → keratinocyte malignancy; melanocyte transformation causes melanoma
AK represents dysplastic keratinocytes with potential progression to invasive SCC

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious melanoma → **full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins** to measure Breslow depth
Partial biopsy acceptable when complete excision impractical; avoid superficial sampling that prevents staging
Suspected keratinocyte carcinoma → deep shave or punch biopsy; <1 cm → **narrow-margin excisional biopsy**
AK persisting after topical fluorouracil → **excisional biopsy** to exclude invasive SCC
Breslow thickness/ulceration guide melanoma staging; sentinel-node discussion generally at ≥0.8 mm or ulceration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized invasive cancers → **surgical excision**; high-risk/recurrent facial BCC/SCC → Mohs
Low-risk BCC → **excision with narrow margins (≤1 cm)**; no sentinel node biopsy
Positive margin on BCC/SCC → **reexcision** or Mohs, not observation
★ Melanoma → **wide local excision after diagnostic biopsy**; margins depend on depth
Advanced melanoma → specialist immunotherapy, selected BRAF-targeted drugs; avoid destructive treatment before diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: BCC: extensive local destruction, rare metastasis; SCC: nodal metastasis, especially high-risk sites/immunosuppression
Melanoma: distant metastases, including brain; immunotherapy → colitis, endocrinopathies, pneumonitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Broad-spectrum SPF ≥30**, reapply every 2 hours/outdoors after swimming; shade, protective clothing, no tanning
Infants <6 months → **shade, protective clothing**; avoid sunscreen
Self-examination, postcancer follow-up; suspicious lesions require evaluation despite uncertain population-screening benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seborrheic keratosis: waxy stuck-on plaque; atypical lesions still biopsy
Dermatofibroma: firm papule with dimple sign
Benign nevus: stable symmetric uniform, <6 mm → **observation**, even with melanoma family history
Congenital melanocytic nevus: brown lesion from birth, may darken or grow coarse hair

table.title: Nonmelanoma patterns
rows: Nonhealing scaly indurated plaque/ulcer/nodule; lip/ear common
Assess high-risk features and regional nodes
Pearly rolled edge, telangiectasia, central ulcer
Treat despite slow growth; local invasion

skin-cancer.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AAD melanoma guidance](https://www.aad.org/member/clinical-quality/guidelines/melanoma); established keratinocyte-cancer and photoprotection teaching.

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics
Functional blindness: intact **pupillary reflex, threat blink, optokinetic nystagmus**
Extreme fever + normal pulse/labs → suspect falsification; **supervised rectal temperature** before antibiotics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic: **incompatible signs**: Hoover, give-way weakness, midline sensory split, forehead vibration discrepancy
Nonepileptic seizures: captured spell without **video-EEG** epileptiform change; often acute stressor
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression
Functional deficits → empathic explanation, expected recovery; nonepileptic seizures → **CBT**, no antiseizure drugs
★ Functional deficit or negative workups → **psychiatric assessment**, no more procedures; **new red flags → reassess**
Factitious: team approach, factual records, no confrontation, evaluate psychiatric comorbidity; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
Factitious disorder imposed on another → serious abuse risk requiring safeguarding action

rows.label: Mimics
items: Occult medical disease: evolving objective findings or coherent physiologic abnormalities
Delusional disorder: fixed somatic belief despite evidence, without flexible doubt

table.title: Distinguishing patterns
rows: Motor/sensory symptoms incompatible with neurologic disease
Intentional deception; no obvious external reward
Intentional symptoms, external gain; no treatment/invasive testing

somatic-symptom-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

stable-ischemic-heart-disease.name: Stable ischemic heart disease
stable-ischemic-heart-disease.scope: Stable angina pectoris, exercise stress testing, stress echocardiography, antianginal pharmacotherapy, invasive coronary angiography indications
stable-ischemic-heart-disease.core: Predictable exertional chest pressure relieved by rest reflects myocardial oxygen supply–demand mismatch; new rest symptoms require acute coronary syndrome evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, older age, family history of premature CAD
Anemia, tachycardia, and uncontrolled blood pressure can worsen ischemic symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Substernal squeezing, arm/jaw radiation; dyspnea or exertional indigestion may be anginal equivalents
Normal resting ECG does not exclude CAD; examination often normal between episodes
★ **Crescendo symptoms, prolonged pain, rest pain**, instability → ECG/troponins and ACS pathway

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Flow-limiting coronary atherosclerosis restricts supply when demand rises
Microvascular dysfunction can produce ischemia despite absence of obstructive epicardial disease

rows.label: Dx
items: Resting ECG, lipid profile, HbA1c, renal function; estimate clinical likelihood before choosing testing
★ Selected intermediate-risk suspected CAD → **CCTA or stress testing**, based on suitability
★ **Coronary angiography** for high-risk noninvasive findings, refractory limiting symptoms, or suspected high-risk anatomy
Stable on medical therapy, low-risk ischemia → no repeat testing or mandatory catheterization; respect informed refusal
Sedentary, risk factors, starting vigorous exercise: no routine stress test; older exam questions may expect exercise ECG

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Relief → **sublingual nitroglycerin**; avoid with recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or hypotension
★ Prevention → **aspirin + high-intensity statin**; manage BP/diabetes, lifestyle and exercise
Antianginal first-line: beta blocker or calcium-channel blocker; persistent symptoms → long-acting nitrate or ranolazine
Beta blockers improve outcomes for selected recent MI/reduced EF indications, not all stable CAD indefinitely
Refractory symptoms → revascularization; CABG improves survival in left-main/selected complex multivessel disease

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, heart failure, malignant arrhythmia, sudden death
Nitrates → headache/hypotension; combining beta blocker with verapamil/diltiazem can cause bradycardia/heart block

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, Mediterranean-style diet, habitual activity; cardiac rehabilitation when eligible
ACE inhibitor/ARB when hypertension, diabetes, CKD, or reduced EF; adherence and lipid follow-up
Drug-eluting stent → **aspirin + clopidogrel**, not anticoagulant; stable CAD 6 months; older exam questions may expect 12

rows.label: Mimics
items: GERD: meal/recumbency association, regurgitation
Aortic stenosis: exertional symptoms with systolic murmur
Costochondritis: reproducible focal chest-wall tenderness
Variant (Prinzmetal) vasospasm: rest/nocturnal pain, **transient ST elevation**, nitrate relief, normal angiography → calcium-channel blocker

table.title: Functional test selection
rows: Exercise stress echocardiography or perfusion imaging

stable-ischemic-heart-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC chronic coronary disease guideline summary (2023)](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2023/07/17/19/06/2023-guideline-for-chronic-coronary-disease-gl-ccd/).

stridor.name: Stridor
stridor.scope: Laryngomalacia (inspiratory, worse supine), tracheomalacia (expiratory), vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical adduction), vascular ring (biphasic, dysphagia), flexible laryngoscopy
stridor.core: Harsh upper-airway noise: respiratory phase localizes obstruction; age, feeding difficulty, and episodic triggers identify the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Congenital airway abnormalities in infancy; prematurity, prior intubation, tracheoesophageal fistula → tracheal weakness
Exercise, stress, irritants → inducible laryngeal obstruction; aortic arch anomalies → extrinsic compression

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Retractions, cyanosis, apnea, exhaustion, or poor air movement** → impending respiratory failure
Feeding-associated choking, recurrent pneumonia, or poor growth → clinically significant obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inspiratory: extrathoracic collapse; expiratory: intrathoracic collapse; biphasic: fixed central obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable unexplained upper-airway noise → **awake flexible laryngoscopy**
Dynamic bronchoscopy assesses distal collapse; CT angiography/MR angiography delineates vascular compression
Normal examination between episodes does not exclude inducible obstruction; visualize during symptoms/exercise
Flow-volume loop: flattened inspiratory limb supports variable extrathoracic obstruction; not definitive alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Distress → oxygen, minimize agitation, **urgent controlled airway** with anesthesia/ENT
Mild congenital malacia → observation, feeding assessment, upright feeding while awake; spontaneous improvement with growth
★ Severe laryngeal collapse with apnea/poor growth → **supraglottoplasty**
Severe tracheal collapse → CPAP; refractory disease → airway surgery
Inducible obstruction → speech-guided breathing; symptomatic vascular ring → surgical division

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxemia, aspiration, recurrent respiratory infections, growth failure; severe obstruction → arrest
Misdiagnosed inducible obstruction → unnecessary bronchodilators, glucocorticoids, or intubations

rows.label: Prevention
items: Supine sleep on flat surface despite positional noise; no prone sleeping or wedges
Avoid smoke exposure; swallowing assessment and feeding modifications reduce aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Croup: acute barky cough after URI; responds to dexamethasone
Foreign body: abrupt choking; rigid bronchoscopy despite normal radiograph
Epiglottitis: fever, drooling, tripod posture; avoid upsetting child or bedside throat examination

table.title: Chronic or episodic causes
rows: Expiratory; barking cough, worsens with exertion
Biphasic wheeze, dysphagia; steroid-unresponsive; neck extension relieves

study-designs.name: Study designs
study-designs.scope: Case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, RCT, control selection, bias, internal and external validity
study-designs.core: Study design determines how participants are selected, when exposure/outcome are measured, and which associations can be estimated without avoidable bias.

rows.label: Definition
items: Internal validity: credible within-study inference; external validity: applicability elsewhere
**Selection/ascertainment bias**: institutional or already-ill sample misrepresents target population
Subjective scoring by different raters → **interobserver variability**; standardize criteria

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Randomization balances confounders on average**; concealed allocation prevents enrollment bias
Blinding reduces behavior/assessment bias; intention-to-treat retains original randomized groups
Loss to follow-up can bias estimates when related to exposure and outcome

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Case-control controls → **same source population** that produced cases, independent of exposure
Prospective measurement improves temporality but does not eliminate confounding in observational research
Life table: poorest 1-year survival → steepest interval drop, not lowest cumulative point

rows.label: Compare
items: Confounding: third-variable distortion; randomize, restrict, match, stratify, or adjust
Effect modification: association differs across strata; report rather than remove it
Clinician-chosen treatment → **selection bias/confounding by indication**; randomization prevents it

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Case-control sampling cannot directly estimate incidence or risk** without additional population data
★ Cross-sectional data lack reliable **temporal sequence**; prevalent cases favor longer survivors
Random selection supports generalizability; random assignment supports causal inference

study-designs.evidence: Established epidemiologic definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

suicide-risk-assessment.name: Suicide risk assessment
suicide-risk-assessment.scope: Risk and protective factors, lethal means restriction, hospitalization criteria, safety planning
suicide-risk-assessment.core: Assess current suicidal intent, plan, access, past behavior, and ability to remain safe; imminent danger requires immediate protection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior attempt strongest historical predictor; depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, substance use, chronic pain
Recent loss, isolation, incarceration/discharge, agitation, hopelessness, firearm access; older men have high fatality risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Plan + intent + available lethal means**, preparations, or recent attempt → high acute risk
Command hallucinations, intoxication, severe insomnia, impulsivity, inability to collaborate increase concern
Giving away possessions or sudden calm after despair can signal resolved intent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Acute distress, impaired judgment, and accessible lethal methods can convert transient suicidal urges into fatal acts
Protective connections and restricted means increase time and opportunity for intervention

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ask directly** about ideation, intent, plan, timing, access, prior attempts; asking does not induce suicide
Depression or hopelessness, even with somatic complaints → assess suicide risk **before further medical workup**
Assess depression/mania, psychosis, substance use, violence risk, medical contributors, collateral information
Use structured instruments to support assessment, never as a sole disposition rule
Intoxicated patient → observation and reassessment when clinically sober; initial denial is insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **constant observation, remove hazards, emergency psychiatric evaluation/hospitalization**
Voluntary admission preferred; involuntary protection if serious danger and refusal, following local law
Treat poisoning/injury first; address agitation, withdrawal, mood/psychotic disorder and underlying medical illness
Low acute risk with reliable support → outpatient care only with collaborative plan and rapid follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Fatal or repeated attempts, hypoxic injury, disability, caregiver distress
High vulnerability after emergency/inpatient discharge; abrupt loss of contact raises concern

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safety plan**: warning signs, coping actions, supportive contacts, professional crisis resources, emergency escalation
★ **Lethal means restriction**: secure/remove firearms, limit medication quantities; enlist trusted support
Arrange prompt follow-up and active care linkage; identify reasons for living and dependable supervision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonsuicidal self-injury: no intent to die, but future suicide risk still elevated
Passive death wish: no active plan, still warrants full evaluation
Obsessive intrusive harm thoughts: unwanted/ego-dystonic, without desire or intent to act

suicide-risk-assessment.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical suicide-risk assessment and safety-planning principles; detention law varies locally.

systemic-vasculitis.name: Systemic vasculitis
systemic-vasculitis.scope: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3), microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA/MPO), eosinophilic GPA, polyarteritis nodosa, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, immunosuppressive therapy
systemic-vasculitis.core: Vessel inflammation presenting as unexplained multisystem ischemia: vessel size, organ pattern, antibodies and tissue distinguish the syndromes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; hydralazine/propylthiouracil can induce ANCA disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Constitutional symptoms, palpable purpura, skin ulcers, mononeuritis multiplex
★ **Hemoptysis + falling hemoglobin + RBC casts** → pulmonary–renal emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ANCA disease → pauci-immune necrotizing injury; larger-vessel inflammation → stenosis, thrombosis, aneurysms
Granulomas: GPA/EGPA, GCA/Takayasu; PAN: necrotizing medium-artery inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis, creatinine, CBC/differential, ESR/CRP**, chest imaging, hepatitis serologies
PR3/MPO supports diagnosis; negative ANCA cannot exclude, isolated positive cannot confirm
★ **Biopsy involved tissue**, especially kidney with GN; do not delay emergency therapy
GCA → temporal artery biopsy/expert ultrasound; **steroids before confirmation**
Takayasu → CTA/MRA; PAN → biopsy or visceral angiography showing microaneurysms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Organ-threatening disease → **urgent immunosuppression**; stabilize bleeding, renal failure, ischemia
GPA/MPA maintenance → rituximab/azathioprine; methotrexate if renal function permits
Plasma exchange not routine in ANCA; consider severe renal disease/anti-GBM overlap
GCA steroid sparing → tocilizumab; elective vascular reconstruction after inflammation controlled
HCV cryoglobulinemia → **direct-acting antivirals**, not immunosuppression alone; older questions may expect interferon-alfa

rows.label: Complications
items: Blindness, renal failure, stroke, bowel infarction, aortic aneurysm
Cyclophosphamide → infertility/cystitis/malignancy; rituximab → HBV reactivation; steroids → infection/osteoporosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **TMP-SMX** with cyclophosphamide/rituximab induction; HBV/TB testing before biologics
Vaccination, bone protection, fertility counseling; follow clinical findings, not ANCA titers alone

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endocarditis: positive blood cultures/vegetations; ANCA sometimes positive
Anti-GBM: linear IgG on renal biopsy
Cholesterol emboli: vascular procedure, blue toes, eosinophilia, preserved pulses

table.title: Disease signatures
rows: PR3/c-ANCA; destructive sinonasal/ear disease, cavitary lungs, GN
Severe disease: same induction as GPA
Steroids; severe → cyclophosphamide; nonsevere relapsing → mepolizumab
Age >50; jaw claudication, visual symptoms, PMR
Young women; pulse/BP discrepancy, arm claudication

testicular-torsion.name: Testicular torsion
testicular-torsion.scope: Testicular torsion, absent cremasteric reflex, bell-clapper deformity, Doppler ultrasound, surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
testicular-torsion.core: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain with vomiting in an adolescent is spermatic cord torsion until excluded; salvage depends on immediate action.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Bell-clapper deformity permits excessive intravaginal rotation; often bilateral anatomic predisposition
Pubertal peak; may follow sleep, activity, or minor trauma; neonates can have extravaginal torsion

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **High-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex**, diffuse tenderness and swelling
Pain may present as lower abdominal discomfort without volunteered scrotal symptoms
Prior self-resolving attacks suggest intermittent torsion; symptom resolution does not eliminate recurrence risk
Delayed fever/erythema can occur; no single examination finding reliably excludes torsion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cord rotation obstructs venous drainage then arterial inflow → progressive ischemia
Viability falls rapidly with delay; greatest salvage when detorsion occurs within about 6 hours

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High clinical suspicion → **immediate urologic exploration**, no imaging delay
Equivocal presentation → **color Doppler ultrasound**, comparing perfusion with opposite testis
Reduced/absent flow or twisted cord supports diagnosis; preserved flow possible in partial/intermittent torsion
Urinalysis for infection if uncertain; pyuria does not automatically exclude simultaneous torsion
Examine both testes in boys with unexplained acute abdominal pain; ultrasound cannot overrule compelling clinical findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Urgent surgical detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy**; orchiectomy only if nonviable
NPO, IV analgesia, fluids as needed; call urology while preparing operation
★ If surgical delay unavoidable → **manual outward detorsion** as bridge; direction sometimes reversed
Pain relief after manual detorsion still requires operative confirmation and fixation; residual twisting possible

rows.label: Complications
items: Infarction, testicular loss, later atrophy, reduced fertility; endocrine function often maintained by opposite testis
Reperfusion does not guarantee long-term viability; follow-up for atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contralateral fixation addresses shared anatomy; evaluate recurrent episodic scrotal pain promptly
Teach adolescents to report sudden pain immediately despite embarrassment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Epididymitis: gradual pain, urinary/STI symptoms, increased epididymal Doppler flow
Appendix testis torsion: focal superior-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign, preserved testicular flow
Incarcerated hernia: irreducible inguinoscrotal mass, possible bowel obstruction

testicular-torsion.evidence: Not checked online; established urologic emergency assessment and salvage principles.

thrombocytopenia.name: Thrombocytopenia
thrombocytopenia.scope: Evaluation of isolated thrombocytopenia, peripheral smear, immune thrombocytopenia, drug-induced, procedural platelet thresholds
thrombocytopenia.core: Low platelet count requires confirmation and distinction among impaired production, immune destruction, consumption, sequestration, and laboratory artifact.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent infection, autoimmune disease, HIV/HCV, lymphoproliferative disease → secondary immune thrombocytopenia
Heparin, quinine, TMP-SMX, vancomycin; alcohol, marrow-suppressive drugs; cirrhosis with splenic sequestration

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding; mucosal hemorrhage signals clinically important platelet disorder
★ **Neurologic/renal abnormalities + hemolysis** → thrombotic microangiopathy; systemic illness/coagulopathy → DIC
Heparin exposure + >50% platelet decline, thrombosis, typical 5–10-day onset → HIT

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ITP: IgG platelet clearance, impaired megakaryocytes; maternal IgG crosses placenta → **fetal platelet destruction**
Drug-dependent immune destruction often causes abrupt severe counts; HIT: anti-PF4/heparin IgG activates platelets, producing thrombosis
**Kasabach-Merritt**: infant vascular tumor (kaposiform hemangioendothelioma/tufted angioma; older exams: hemangioma) traps platelets → severe thrombocytopenia, consumptive coagulopathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Repeat CBC + peripheral smear**; platelet clumps → citrate tube for pseudothrombocytopenia
Isolated low platelets, normal coagulation, large platelets → ITP after excluding secondary causes
Schistocytes → LDH, haptoglobin, creatinine, coagulation studies; suspected TTP → urgent ADAMTS13 sample
HIV/HCV testing for new ITP; marrow biopsy only atypical cytopenias or suspected marrow disease
4Ts estimates HIT probability; intermediate/high → PF4 immunoassay, functional confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult ITP **<30,000/µL or bleeding → glucocorticoid**; children without significant bleeding → observation
★ ITP critical bleeding → **IVIG + high-dose steroid + platelet transfusion**
Drug immune thrombocytopenia → stop culprit; persistent ITP → rituximab, thrombopoietin agonist, or selected splenectomy
Suspected TTP → plasma exchange; HIT → stop heparin, start argatroban/nonheparin anticoagulant
Older board LP target: 50,000/µL; current trigger below; neurosurgical targets often ≥100,000/µL

rows.label: Complications
items: Intracranial hemorrhage with severe disease; thrombosis in HIT/TTP
Steroid toxicity, immunosuppression; splenectomy → encapsulated bacterial sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid culprit rechallenge, aspirin/NSAIDs when bleeding risk high; vaccinate before splenectomy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Von Willebrand disease: often normal platelet count with mucocutaneous bleeding
Marrow failure: additional cytopenias, abnormal precursor morphology

thrombocytopenia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AABB/ICTMG platelet recommendations (2025)](https://www.aabb.org/news-resources/news/article/2025/05/29/aabb-develops-new-platelet-transfusion-guidelines); other hematology principles not separately checked.

thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.name: Thyroid nodules and cancer
thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.scope: Evaluation (TSH, ultrasound, FNA), benign goiter (multinodular goiter, compressive symptoms), thyroid cancer types
thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.core: A thyroid nodule requires functional assessment and ultrasound risk stratification; suspicious nonfunctioning nodules require cytologic evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childhood head/neck irradiation, familial thyroid cancer, MEN 2
Multinodular goiter: iodine deficiency, age; multiple nodules do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Hard fixed lesion, cervical nodes, rapid growth or persistent hoarseness increase cancer concern
Large benign goiter → dysphagia, positional dyspnea, tracheal compression
Anaplastic cancer: older adult with rapidly enlarging invasive neck mass

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Follicular-derived tumors differ in differentiation and spread; C-cell tumors produce calcitonin
Autonomous nodules synthesize hormone without pituitary stimulation and rarely contain malignancy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable nodule → **TSH and thyroid ultrasound** first; document cervical nodes and suspicious features
★ Low TSH → radionuclide scan; hot nodule generally **no FNA**
Normal/high TSH → ultrasound-guided FNA by sonographic risk and size
High/intermediate suspicion ≥1 cm → FNA; low suspicion ≥1.5 cm; very low suspicion ≥2 cm
★ Follicular neoplasm on FNA → diagnostic lobectomy; **capsular/vascular invasion** requires histology

rows.label: Tx
items: Benign asymptomatic nodule → ultrasound follow-up; compressive or substernal goiter → surgery
Differentiated cancer → lobectomy/thyroidectomy by risk; selected higher-risk cases → radioactive iodine
★ Medullary cancer → thyroidectomy; evaluate **pheochromocytoma before surgery**
Anaplastic disease → airway planning, multidisciplinary systemic/local treatment; radioiodine ineffective

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness; bilateral injury → airway obstruction
Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia; expanding hematoma → emergency decompression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary neck radiation; RET-positive families → counseling and preventive thyroidectomy planning
Asymptomatic adult: **no routine ultrasound**; USPSTF against average-risk screening; older questions may expect palpation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Thyroiditis: tenderness or inflammatory history, transient dysfunction
Thyroglossal cyst: midline mass moves with tongue protrusion

table.title: Cancer signatures
rows: Orphan Annie nuclei; psammoma bodies; lymphatic spread

thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established ATA nodule evaluation and board-level management.

type-2-diabetes-mellitus.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
type-2-diabetes-mellitus.scope: Diagnosis, glycemic targets, pharmacotherapy (metformin contraindications, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA, insulin), chronic complications screening, pediatric screening in obesity
type-2-diabetes-mellitus.core: Insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure produces chronic hyperglycemia and vascular injury, often preceding obvious symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central obesity, family history, prior gestational diabetes, PCOS, physical inactivity
Glucocorticoids and atypical antipsychotics can unmask dysglycemia

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, recurrent candidiasis; acanthosis nigricans suggests marked insulin resistance
Weight loss, ketosis, or dehydration → severe insulin deficiency; reconsider diabetes type

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired glucose uptake + excess hepatic output; early compensatory **↑serum insulin**, later relative secretory failure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **A1c ≥6.5%**, fasting glucose ≥126, or 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL
Random glucose ≥200 with classic symptoms also diagnostic; otherwise confirm with second abnormal result
A1c unreliable with altered erythrocyte survival; use plasma glucose
★ Youth: screen puberty/age 10, whichever earlier, with overweight/obesity + additional risk; repeat ≥every 2 years

rows.label: Tx
items: Lifestyle + metformin; **lactic acidosis**: avoid eGFR <30, AKI/sepsis, hypoxia; no new start <45; reduce 30–44
★ HF/CKD → **SGLT2 inhibitor**; ASCVD/obesity → GLP-1 RA, independent of A1c or metformin
★ Catabolism, glucose ≥300, or A1c >10% → **insulin**
Otherwise GLP-1 RA before insulin; older exam questions may expect **basal insulin** once two orals fail
Adults: A1c <7%, fasting 80–130, postmeal <180; relax for frailty/hypoglycemia; quarterly checks until stable

rows.label: Complications
items: Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, foot ulceration; coronary, cerebral, and peripheral arterial disease
SGLT2 inhibitors: genital mycoses, euglycemic DKA; sulfonylureas/insulin: hypoglycemia, weight gain
Metformin: GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; pioglitazone: edema, HF; sulfonylureas: labeled caution with sulfa allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ At diagnosis then annually: **urine albumin/creatinine, eGFR, foot and dilated eye examinations** (eye spacing by findings)
★ Albuminuria + hypertension → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**, never both; efferent dilation ↓intraglomerular pressure
BP ≥130/80 → antihypertensive; older exam questions may expect ACE inhibitor, also normotensive albuminuria
Statin age 40–75; glycemic control slows **neuropathy**, retinopathy, nephropathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Type 1 diabetes: autoantibodies, low C-peptide, abrupt ketosis
Diabetes insipidus: dilute polyuria without elevated blood glucose

umbilical-cord-prolapse.name: Umbilical cord prolapse
umbilical-cord-prolapse.scope: Overt vs occult prolapse, risk factors (unengaged presenting part, polyhydramnios, artificial rupture of membranes, malpresentation), sudden fetal bradycardia, manual elevation of fetal head, emergent cesarean delivery
umbilical-cord-prolapse.core: Sudden fetal bradycardia or severe variable decelerations after membrane rupture requires immediate examination for a compressed prolapsed cord.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High/unengaged presenting part, breech/transverse lie, prematurity, polyhydramnios, multiple gestation
Amniotomy or manipulation when presenting part not well applied to cervix

rows.label: Clues
items: Visible/palpable pulsatile structure in vagina; abrupt tracing deterioration may be only sign
Cord can lose pulsation with severe compression; absence of pulse does not establish fetal death

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Presenting part compresses vessels; exposed cord may vasospasm → abrupt reduction of fetal oxygen delivery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Immediate vaginal examination** after suspicious tracing change, especially following rupture
Clinical diagnosis; ultrasound can assess viability when uncertain but must not delay intervention
Continuously monitor fetal heart rate; document time, maneuvers, and response

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Call help; **manually elevate presenting part** off cord and maintain elevation until birth
★ Knee-chest or head-down lateral positioning; stop oxytocin; relieve compression while preparing delivery
★ **Emergency cesarean** unless fully dilated with immediate safe vaginal/operative vaginal birth possible
Minimize cord handling; exposed loop → warm saline-moistened gauze; do not attempt routine cord replacement
Transfer delay → bladder filling via catheter ± terbutaline; decompression never substitutes for definitive birth

rows.label: Complications
items: Fetal acidemia, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, stillbirth; emergency delivery increases maternal surgical risk
Residual neurologic injury depends on compression severity and duration

rows.label: Prevention
items: Confirm presenting part engaged before amniotomy; controlled rupture for selected high-risk cases
Known unstable lie at term → planned obstetric management and prompt assessment after spontaneous rupture

rows.label: Mimics
items: Placental abruption: painful bleeding, hypertonic tender uterus; concealed bleeding possible
Maternal hypotension: occurs after epidural/supine positioning, no cord on examination
Vasa previa rupture: vaginal bleeding with fetal deterioration from fetal blood loss

table.title: Cord position
rows: Cord below presenting part after membrane rupture
Cord alongside presenting part; not externally visible
Cord between presenting part and cervix before rupture

urinary-retention.name: Urinary retention
urinary-retention.scope: Acute vs chronic urinary retention, postoperative etiology, neurogenic bladder, medication-induced, postrenal acute kidney injury, post-void residual volume, bladder catheterization decompression
urinary-retention.core: Inability to empty the bladder requires prompt decompression, identification of obstruction or impaired detrusor function, and monitoring after relief.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: BPH, urethral stricture, prolapse, constipation/fecal impaction, pelvic mass
Surgery/anesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics (diphenhydramine), sympathomimetics; childbirth, diabetic neuropathy, spinal disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute: painful suprapubic fullness, inability to void, palpable bladder; postoperative discomfort may be muted
Chronic: hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, recurrent infection, overflow dribbling
★ **Back pain, saddle anesthesia, leg weakness** → cauda equina emergency; painless retention can be neurogenic

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Outlet resistance or deficient detrusor contraction leaves residual urine, raising intravesical pressure
Persistent high pressure transmits to ureters/kidneys → hydronephrosis and postrenal AKI

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bladder scan/postvoid residual** immediately; catheter measurement if scan unavailable or unreliable
PVR >200 mL suggests incomplete emptying; >300–400 supports retention, but acute diagnosis remains clinical
Urinalysis, creatinine/electrolytes; renal ultrasound for renal dysfunction or suspected chronic high-pressure obstruction
Focused medication, neurologic, rectal/pelvic examination; urgent spinal MRI for compressive neurologic signs
Blood at urethral meatus after pelvic trauma → retrograde urethrogram before blind catheterization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Urethral catheter decompression** promptly; difficult passage → experienced placement, sometimes suprapubic catheter
★ Drain completely; **routine intermittent clamping unnecessary**; monitor hematuria, BP, urine output
BPH → tamsulosin before trial without catheter; stop offending drugs, treat constipation or infection
Neurogenic/chronic incomplete emptying → clean intermittent catheterization when feasible; address obstruction definitively
Postobstructive diuresis >200 mL/hour for 2 hours or >3 L/day → fluids/electrolyte monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: UTI, bladder damage, hydronephrosis, kidney injury; catheter → infection/urethral trauma
After decompression: hypovolemia, electrolyte loss, transient bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review anticholinergic/opioid burden, mobilize postoperatively; voiding trials and early catheter removal when safe

rows.label: Mimics
items: Prerenal/intrinsic oliguria: low bladder volume rather than distended reservoir
Urge incontinence: urgency/leakage with low residual, unlike overflow retention

urinary-retention.evidence: Decompression/diuresis checked 2026-10-30: [AUA urologic emergencies](https://www.auanet.org/Documents/education/medical%20student%20curriculum/Urologic-%20Emergencies-AUA-Med-Student.pdf); remaining content established teaching.

urinary-tract-infections.name: Urinary tract infections
urinary-tract-infections.scope: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), catheter removal, empiric antibiotics
urinary-tract-infections.core: Symptoms localize urinary infection: bladder disease lacks systemic illness; renal involvement causes fever or flank pain; bacteriuria alone is insufficient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual activity, spermicides, pregnancy, obstruction/stones, urinary retention, instrumentation
Catheter duration, diabetes, prior resistant isolates or antibiotics increase complicated-course risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort; absent vaginal discharge supports urinary source
★ **Rigors, CVA tenderness, vomiting, hypotension** → pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Catheterized patients: new urinary/systemic symptoms; cloudy urine or pyuria alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually ascending enteric bacteria, predominantly E coli; catheter biofilm maintains colonization
Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine → struvite calculi and persistent infection
Pregnancy: progesterone ureteral relaxation + uterine compression → **stasis**; physiologic right-sided ureteral dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**: pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites; pyelonephritis → heavy pyuria, WBC clumps/casts; negative nitrites don't exclude
Culture: pyelonephritis, pregnancy, CAUTI, recurrence/resistance; classic cystitis often clinical
Persistent fever after 48–72 hours, sepsis, or suspected obstruction → renal imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: usually ≥100,000 CFU/mL; delirium alone → seek other causes without automatic antibiotics
Febrile non-toilet-trained child → **catheterized** urinalysis/culture; bag/clean-catch contaminate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before urologic mucosal trauma** in routine adult scenarios
★ CAUTI → **remove unnecessary catheter**; if needed and present >2 weeks, replace before culture/treatment
★ Infected obstructed collecting system → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics**; antibiotics alone insufficient
Improving nonpregnant pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone 5–7 days, other active drugs 7 days; high-risk cases individualized
Febrile infant → **cefotaxime/ceftriaxone**; first-generation cefazolin inadequate

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, septic shock, renal/perinephric abscess; pregnancy → preterm birth
Antibiotics → resistance, C difficile; fluoroquinolones → tendon injury, QT prolongation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary catheters; closed drainage, daily removal assessment
Postmenopausal recurrence → vaginal estrogen
Recurrence ≥3/year or ≥2 in 6 months → postcoital or daily nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX
Sporadic postcoital cystitis → **void before/after intercourse**; stop diaphragm/spermicide; condoms don't prevent

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vaginitis: discharge, pruritus, external burning
Urethritis: sexual exposure, discharge, positive gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Bladder pain syndrome: chronic symptoms, repeatedly negative cultures

table.title: Initial antibiotics; tailor to culture/resistance
rows: Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; initial ceftriaxone if resistance risk
IV fluids + ceftriaxone; cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam if Pseudomonas risk
Avoid nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin: inadequate renal tissue levels

viral-hepatitis.name: Viral hepatitis
viral-hepatitis.scope: Hepatitis A, B, C, D, E, serologic markers, acute vs chronic hepatitis, HCV antibody and RNA confirmatory testing, direct-acting antivirals, postexposure prophylaxis (HBIG and vaccine)
viral-hepatitis.core: Hepatocellular injury with malaise, anorexia, jaundice, and high aminotransferases prompts exposure-based viral testing; chronic infection may be clinically silent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HAV/HEV: fecal–oral spread; HBV/HCV/HDV: blood, perinatal exposure; HBV also sexual
Injection exposure, unscreened blood, endemic birth region; HDV requires HBV
HEV severe in pregnancy; perinatal HBV and most untreated HCV often become chronic

rows.label: Clues
items: Dark urine, pale stool, RUQ discomfort; transaminases often far exceed alkaline phosphatase
★ **Encephalopathy + INR ≥1.5 without preexisting cirrhosis** → acute liver failure
HBV: serum sickness, polyarteritis nodosa; HCV: mixed cryoglobulinemia, porphyria cutanea tarda

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Host immune injury to infected hepatocytes; persistent HBV/HCV → fibrosis and carcinogenesis
HBV nuclear templates persist; HCV cure does not confer immunity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ HAV acute → **IgM anti-HAV**; total/IgG antibody indicates immunity
★ **HCV antibody → reflex HCV RNA**; antibody persists after clearance; recent exposure → RNA directly
HBsAg persisting >6 months → chronic HBV; HBV DNA quantifies replication
HEV testing by exposure/context; HBsAg-positive severe hepatitis → consider anti-HDV/HDV RNA
INR, bilirubin, creatinine; chronic disease → fibrosis staging, coinfection testing

rows.label: Tx
items: HAV, most HEV, uncomplicated acute HBV → supportive care; liver failure → urgent transplant center
★ Chronic HCV → **glecaprevir/pibrentasvir or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir**, usually 8–12 weeks; verify interactions/cirrhosis
Chronic HBV needing treatment → tenofovir or entecavir; severe acute HBV also may need antiviral
HCV cure: RNA undetectable ≥12 weeks after completion; do not delay treatment awaiting spontaneous resolution

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant hepatitis; chronic HBV/HCV → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma
HBV can cause HCC without cirrhosis; DAAs may reactivate unrecognized HBV
Cirrhosis/selected HBV → HCC surveillance with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Susceptible HBV exposure → **HBIG + vaccine promptly**, preferably within 24 h; immunity determines exceptions
Newborn ≥2,000 g, maternal HBsAg unknown → vaccine ≤12 h; HBIG only if mother positive
HAV exposure ≤2 weeks → vaccine; add immune globulin for immunocompromise/chronic liver disease
HAV/HBV vaccines, safer sex/injection practices; no HCV vaccine or proven HCV PEP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Drug-induced injury: medication/toxin relationship
Ischemic hepatitis: shock preceding abrupt marked aminotransferase rise

vulvar-cancer.name: Vulvar cancer
vulvar-cancer.scope: Squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma of the vulva, lichen sclerosus malignant transformation, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), Paget disease of the vulva, staging, wide local excision, sentinel node biopsy
vulvar-cancer.core: Persistent vulvar pruritus with a focal ulcer, plaque, or mass requires biopsy, especially in an older patient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HPV-related disease: smoking, immunosuppression; HPV-independent disease: older age, lichen sclerosus
Prior vulvar HSIL/VIN; chronic symptoms repeatedly treated without tissue diagnosis delay detection
Prior cervical neoplasia: HPV field risk; new vulvar mass → primary cancer, metastasis rare

rows.label: Clues
items: Nonhealing lesion, bleeding, dyspareunia, focal pain; enlarged inguinal nodes suggest regional spread
★ **Changing pigmented lesion** requires melanoma evaluation; amelanotic lesions also occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Squamous carcinoma spreads locally, then to inguinofemoral nodes; nodal involvement strongly influences prognosis
HPV-associated HSIL and HPV-independent differentiated VIN are distinct precursor pathways

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Punch/incisional biopsy** of suspicious lesion; sample viable edge, not only necrotic center
Document lesion size, depth, focality, proximity to midline; examine groin nodes
Suspicious nodes → ultrasound-guided sampling; advanced local extent → pelvic MRI and metastatic imaging
Stage by stromal invasion, adjacent-organ extension, and nodal/distant spread; evaluate multifocal disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized invasive disease → **wide local excision** with negative margins
Microinvasive SCC ≤1 mm stromal invasion generally needs no groin-node surgery
★ Unifocal **<4 cm**, invasion >1 mm, clinically negative nodes → sentinel-node biopsy
Larger/multifocal or node-positive disease → groin treatment; locally advanced → chemoradiation and/or surgery
Paget → excision; VIN → excision, or laser/imiquimod after excluding invasion

rows.label: Complications
items: Local recurrence, nodal metastasis; surgery/radiation → lymphedema, wound breakdown, sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: HPV vaccination, tobacco cessation; high-potency topical corticosteroids for lichen sclerosus, continued surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lichen simplex chronicus: diffuse scratch-induced thickening; biopsy persistent focal changes
Candidiasis: yeast on microscopy, responds to antifungal; persistent lesion still needs sampling

table.title: Histologic clues
rows: Ulcerated/keratotic mass; HPV or inflammatory pathway
Asymmetry, irregular color/border; Breslow depth guides management
Chronic eczematous red plaque; intraepithelial glandular cells

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.scope: Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, oculomotor dysfunction), Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, amnesia), thiamine (B1) deficiency, IV thiamine before glucose, mammillary body atrophy
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.core: Malnourished adult with confusion, gait ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; the complete Wernicke triad is often absent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, starvation, inadequate parenteral nutrition
IV dextrose, carbohydrate loading or refeeding increases thiamine demand → precipitates Wernicke in depleted patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Ocular: nystagmus, **bilateral lateral rectus (CN VI) palsy**, conjugate-gaze palsy; wide-based gait
Hypothermia, hypotension, or coma signal severe deficiency
★ Korsakoff: disproportionate **anterograde amnesia**, retrograde memory loss, confabulation; relatively preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate metabolism → ATP failure and selective neuronal injury
Medial thalami, periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies injured → persistent amnestic syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; do not wait for vitamin assays or imaging before treatment
MRI may show symmetric thalamic/periaqueductal lesions; normal MRI does not exclude Wernicke
Chronic disease: mammillary body atrophy; evaluate glucose, electrolytes, magnesium, and competing encephalopathy causes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke → **high-dose IV thiamine**, followed by oral replacement after stabilization
**IV thiamine before or with dextrose**, hypoglycemia included; if thiamine unavailable, never delay dextrose
Replete magnesium, fluid/electrolyte deficits; restore nutrition cautiously and treat alcohol withdrawal separately
Ocular findings may improve rapidly; gait/cognition recover more slowly; established amnesia often persists

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated encephalopathy → death or irreversible Korsakoff syndrome; falls and impaired independent living
Refeeding syndrome → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmias, respiratory weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Routine oral **thiamine supplementation** for persistent malnutrition; nutritional assessment during alcohol treatment
Alcohol cessation support, balanced nutrition; monitor intake after bariatric surgery or prolonged vomiting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, hallucinations after reduced intake
Hepatic encephalopathy: cirrhosis, asterixis, precipitating bleed or infection
Posterior circulation stroke: abrupt focal deficits; diffusion MRI identifies infarction

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established thiamine-deficiency teaching.
